content.text: The EF Core InMemory provider isn't a database. It runs your LINQ as ordinary C# over in-memory collections, so it skips foreign keys, unique indexes, column lengths and decimal precision, compares strings the C# way, and happily runs queries SQL Server can't translate. Microsoft discourages it for testing. Test your data access against the database engine you ship on, and put test doubles above your data access, not under it.
A sign-up endpoint must reject an email that's already registered, whatever its case. The team's tests use
UseInMemoryDatabase
, and the first version of the check failed the test "rejects
ana@example.com
when
Ana@Example.com
exists". So the developer rewrote the query with
string.Equals(c.Email, email, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
. The test turned green and the change shipped. In production, on SQL Server, every sign-up now fails with
InvalidOperationException: The LINQ expression ... could not be translated
. The fake didn't just miss a bug. It caused one.
The common misconception
The belief: the InMemory provider is a fast, faithful stand-in for the real database. Same
DbContext
, same LINQ, no server to install, no data to clean up, and tests that run in milliseconds.

It's easy to see why teams reach for it. It ships with EF Core and takes one line to configure. Plenty of tutorials and sample test projects use it. For simple add-and-find tests it really does behave like a database, so the first few hundred tests go green and build trust. And a real database in tests sounds slow and fiddly to set up, so a fake that "just works" feels like the pragmatic choice.
What actually happens
It's a list with a DbContext in front

The InMemory provider isn't relational. Microsoft's docs say it was originally designed to support EF Core's own internal testing, that new features aren't being added to it, and that using it as a database fake is "highly discouraged". Your LINQ never becomes SQL: it runs as .NET code over the stored objects. That single fact explains every difference below. In tests with EF Core 10, the same operations ran against InMemory, SQLite in-memory and SQL Server LocalDB.
Constraints the database enforces don't exist
A real database rejects bad data. InMemory stores it.

items.text: an order pointing at customer 999, who doesn't exist, saved on InMemory. SQLite and SQL Server both refused it.
a second customer with the same email saved on InMemory. Both databases threw.
column saved on InMemory and SQLite. SQL Server threw "String or binary data would be truncated".
column read back as 10.555 on InMemory and SQLite, and as 10.56 on SQL Server.

content.text: Each of these is a
DbUpdateException
or a rounding difference your tests will never see.
Queries are judged by C#, not SQL
Because the query runs as C#, string equality is ordinal and case-sensitive. SQL Server's default
collation
is case-insensitive, so
c.Email == "ana@example.com"
found
Ana@Example.com
on SQL Server and found nothing on InMemory. Worse, InMemory accepts expressions a relational provider can't translate.
string.Equals
with
StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase
ran fine on InMemory and threw "could not be translated" on both SQLite and SQL Server.
Whole features are missing
Starting a transaction on InMemory threw an error for
TransactionIgnoredWarning
: transactions aren't supported, and if you suppress the warning they're silently ignored, so a rollback test proves nothing.
FromSql
threw, and so did
ExecuteUpdate

, which only relational providers support. Deleting an order without loading its lines left the lines behind as orphans, because InMemory doesn't support cascade deletes in the database. SQL Server and SQLite deleted them.
It isn't even the fast option

Speed is the usual reason to pick it, and Microsoft's docs say the provider hasn't been optimized for performance and is generally slower than SQLite in-memory, or even than your production database. EF Core itself runs over 30,000 tests against SQL Server, which complete in a few minutes on every commit.
The fix: test the query where it will run

content.text: The right version doesn't depend on any collation, and the unique index makes the database itself reject a duplicate that slips past the check. Then test it against SQL Server, isolating each test in a transaction that's never committed, as Microsoft's testing guide recommends:
The fixture creates the database once per test run with
EnsureDeleted
and
EnsureCreated
. In a test on LocalDB, the check returned
true
, and the table was empty again once the context was disposed.

rows.text: on strings that differ in case

blocks.title: SQLite is a better fake, not the real thing

content.text: SQLite caught the foreign key and unique index violations, but not the length limit, the rounding or the case-insensitive match. Microsoft's docs suggest SQLite in-memory only when neither the real database nor a repository-style test double is practical, and warn that it doesn't guarantee the same results. Use it knowingly, not as the final word on your queries.

blocks.title: Fake above the data access, not under it

content.text: For fast unit tests of business logic, replace the code that runs queries with a
test double
that returns results directly, and leave LINQ out of those tests entirely. Then every query gets its own test against the real engine. That's the split Microsoft's testing guide recommends.
How to apply it in your project
Search your test projects for
UseInMemoryDatabase
and list which tests check queries, constraints or transactions. Those are the ones giving false confidence.
Run the production database in a container, with Testcontainers or your CI's services, or use SQL Server Developer Edition or LocalDB on developer machines.
Create the database once per run, wrap each writing test in a transaction you never commit, and call
ChangeTracker.Clear()
before reading back what you wrote.

items.title: Move logic tests above the queries

content.text: Where you want speed, test business logic against a stubbed interface that returns results, and keep the LINQ in classes that are tested only against the database.
Key takeaways

items.text: The InMemory provider runs LINQ as C# over collections; it was built for EF Core's own tests and Microsoft discourages it as a fake.
It doesn't enforce foreign keys, unique indexes, lengths or precision, and it compares strings with C# rules.
It runs queries that SQL Server can't translate, so a test can pass for code that always fails in production.
and database cascades don't work on it at all.
Test queries against the engine you ship on, isolated with transactions, and stub above the data access for fast logic tests.
